questions.stem: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.explanation: The heart is a muscular pump. The lungs handle gas exchange but do not pump blood.
questions.teaching:
The circulatory system has three parts: a pump, a set of vessels, and the blood itself.

The pump is a muscular organ divided into four chambers, working continuously to push blood in two circuits — one to the lungs to collect oxygen, and one to the rest of the body to deliver it. The lungs do the gas exchange but no pumping. The liver processes what the blood carries. Understanding the two-circuit design is what explains why the organ has four chambers rather than two, and why one side has a much thicker wall than the other.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the digestive system?
options: Removing carbon dioxide from the blood
Breaking food down so nutrients can be absorbed
questions.explanation: Digestion breaks large food molecules into small ones the body can absorb and use.

questions.stem: Which organ system takes oxygen into the body?
questions.explanation: The respiratory system brings air into the lungs where oxygen enters the blood.

questions.stem: Where does most absorption of digested food happen?
questions.explanation: The small intestine is long and lined with villi, giving a huge absorbing surface. The stomach mainly churns and chemically breaks food down.

questions.stem: What does the large intestine mainly absorb?
questions.explanation: By the time material reaches the large intestine, nutrients have largely been absorbed. Water reabsorption is its main role.
questions.teaching:
Digestion happens along a tube, and each section does a different job, so questions usually test which section does what.

The stomach churns food and begins protein digestion in acid. The small intestine is where most chemical digestion finishes and where the products of digestion are absorbed into the blood, through a vast surface area of villi. By the time material reaches the final section, the nutrients are largely gone, and what remains is mostly indigestible fibre and a great deal of fluid. That section reclaims the fluid, which is why dehydration and diarrhoea are linked.

questions.stem: Which organ system includes the brain and spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The brain and spinal cord are the central nervous system, with nerves reaching the rest of the body.

questions.stem: What do the kidneys do?
options: Filter waste from the blood to make urine
questions.explanation: Kidneys filter the blood, removing urea and excess water and salts.

questions.stem: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away; veins bring it back. A useful memory: Arteries — Away.
questions.teaching:
The two main vessel types are distinguished by direction relative to the heart, not by what they carry.

One type carries blood away from the heart. Because that blood has just been pushed out of a powerful chamber, the pressure is high, so these vessels have thick elastic walls — which is why a pulse can be felt in them. The other type returns blood to the heart at much lower pressure, with thinner walls and valves. The common error is defining them by oxygen: the vessel to the lungs carries deoxygenated blood and is still the away-from-heart type.

questions.stem: Where in the lungs does gas exchange take place?
questions.explanation: Alveoli are tiny air sacs with thin walls and a rich blood supply, which is where oxygen and carbon dioxide swap.

questions.stem: Which system supports the body and protects organs?
questions.explanation: Bones give the body its frame and shield organs — the skull protects the brain, the ribs the heart and lungs.

questions.stem: What is peristalsis?
options: The breakdown of food by enzymes
The absorption of water in the large intestine
The movement of air into the lungs
Waves of muscle contraction that push food along the gut
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is muscular squeezing that moves food along, which is why swallowing works even lying down.

questions.stem: Which organ produces bile to help digest fats?
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile, which the gall bladder stores. The pancreas releases digestive enzymes rather than bile.

questions.stem: What is the muscle below the lungs that helps you breathe called?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm flattens to draw air in and relaxes to push it out.

questions.stem: Which part of blood carries oxygen?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin. White cells fight infection and platelets help clotting.

questions.stem: Which system releases hormones into the blood?
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones as chemical messengers. It is slower than the nervous system but longer-lasting.

questions.stem: Why does the small intestine have millions of tiny villi?
options: They increase surface area so absorption is faster
They push food along more quickly
questions.explanation: More surface means more contact between digested food and the blood supply. Movement is peristalsis and bile comes from the liver.

questions.stem: Which two systems work together to deliver oxygen to a working muscle?
questions.explanation: The lungs take oxygen in and the blood carries it to the muscle. Neither system can do the job alone.

questions.stem: Why does breathing rate increase during exercise?
options: The heart stops pumping as hard
The body needs to cool the blood
Muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Working muscles respire faster, using more oxygen and producing more carbon dioxide, so breathing speeds up to keep pace.

questions.stem: Blood leaving the lungs differs from blood entering them. How?
options: It carries more oxygen and less carbon dioxide
It carries more carbon dioxide and less oxygen
It carries oxygen only, with no carbon dioxide left in it
It contains more red blood cells
questions.explanation: Gas exchange in the alveoli loads oxygen and unloads carbon dioxide. The number of red cells does not change.

questions.stem: Why are capillary walls only one cell thick?
options: So blood flows through them faster
So they can carry more blood
So substances can diffuse quickly between blood and tissue
questions.explanation: A short diffusion distance means fast exchange. Capillaries actually slow the blood, which gives exchange more time.

questions.stem: A person's digestive enzymes stop working. What is the most direct effect?
options: Large food molecules are not broken into absorbable ones
questions.explanation: Enzymes do the chemical breakdown. Mechanical processes like swallowing and churning would continue but achieve little on their own.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces air into the body?
options: Nose or mouth, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
questions.explanation: Air passes down the windpipe, branches into bronchi and bronchioles, and ends at the alveoli. The oesophagus carries food, not air.

questions.stem: Why do valves in veins matter?
options: They stop blood flowing backwards where pressure is low
They pump blood towards the heart
They filter waste from the blood
questions.explanation: Blood in veins is under low pressure, so valves prevent backflow. Movement comes from surrounding muscles squeezing the veins, not from the valves pumping.

questions.stem: Which best explains why a multicellular organism needs organ systems?
options: Organ systems replace the need for cells
Specialised systems can carry out functions no single cell could manage for the whole body
Organ systems make an organism heavier
questions.explanation: Size and complexity make division of labour necessary. Organ systems are themselves built from cells, so they do not replace them.

questions.stem: A student says the heart pumps oxygen around the body. What is the better statement?
options: The heart pumps blood, which carries oxygen
questions.explanation: The heart moves blood; the blood is the carrier. Precision matters here because the lungs, not the heart, load the oxygen.

questions.stem: Why does the left side of the heart have a thicker muscular wall than the right?
options: It pumps blood all the way around the body, not just to the lungs
It receives blood from the lungs
It beats more often than the right side
questions.explanation: Higher pressure is needed for the whole-body circuit, so more muscle. Both sides beat together and hold similar volumes.

questions.stem: How do the nervous and muscular systems work together when you catch a ball?
options: Nerves carry signals that make muscles contract at the right moment
Muscles send signals telling nerves what to do
The nervous system moves the arm directly
Muscles detect the ball and decide to move
questions.explanation: Sensing and coordination are nervous system jobs; the movement itself is muscular. The signal travels from nerve to muscle.

questions.stem: What happens to the diaphragm and rib muscles when you breathe in?
options: The diaphragm flattens and the ribs move down and in
The diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out
The diaphragm domes upwards and the ribs move down
questions.explanation: Both actions enlarge the chest cavity, lowering the pressure inside so air flows in. Breathing out is the reverse.

questions.stem: Which observation best shows that organ systems depend on each other?
options: Bones are hard and lungs are soft
Blocked lung function quickly affects muscles all over the body
The heart is inside the ribcage
The stomach is near the liver
questions.explanation: Failure in one system showing up in another demonstrates dependence. Physical proximity does not.

questions.stem: Why can a person survive with one kidney but not with no lungs?
options: The liver can filter blood instead of a kidney
One lung can be replaced by the diaphragm
Kidneys are paired with spare filtering capacity; gas exchange has no alternative organ
Kidneys are less important than lungs
questions.explanation: A single kidney can handle the whole filtering load. There is no other structure that can exchange gases at the rate the body needs.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does. Why is this dangerous?
options: It stops the heart from beating directly
It prevents food from being digested
It causes the lungs to fill with fluid
Red blood cells can no longer carry enough oxygen to the tissues
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is occupied by carbon monoxide, so oxygen cannot be picked up. Breathing and heartbeat may look normal while tissues are starved.

questions.stem: Which explains why the alveoli's structure suits its function so well?
options: They are the largest structures in the lungs
They actively pump oxygen into the blood
Huge combined surface area, thin walls and a dense blood supply maintain a steep diffusion gradient
questions.explanation: Area, thinness and blood flow together maximise diffusion. Gas exchange is passive — nothing is pumped.

questions.stem: A student claims that arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood. Where does this break down?
options: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs
Veins never carry blood to the heart
questions.explanation: The definition is about direction, not oxygen: arteries carry blood away from the heart. The pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are the exceptions to the oxygen pattern.

questions.stem: During heavy exercise, blood is redirected away from the digestive system. Why?
options: The digestive system stops needing oxygen
Blood cannot flow to two places at once
Digestion produces carbon dioxide that must be avoided
Working muscles need a larger share of a limited blood supply
questions.explanation: Blood volume is finite, so priority shifts to where demand is greatest. Digestive organs still need some supply — it is a reduction, not a shut-off.

questions.stem: A drug slows peristalsis. Which effect is most likely?
options: Less water is absorbed, so the waste leaving the gut is looser
Food moves through the gut more slowly and more water is absorbed from it
questions.explanation: Slower movement leaves material in the gut longer, so more water is drawn out of it. Enzyme production and absorption continue.

questions.stem: Why is it more accurate to describe body systems as interacting rather than working separately?
options: All systems are made of the same organ
The systems are physically joined together
Only one system works at a time
Each system depends on materials and signals supplied by others to function at all
questions.explanation: The respiratory system is useless without circulation to distribute oxygen, and muscles are useless without nervous signals. Dependency, not separation, is the rule.

questions.stem: Which finding would most challenge the idea that the kidneys control the body's water balance?
options: Urine becoming more concentrated on a hot day
Drinking more water leading to more urine
Kidneys receiving a large share of the blood supply
Water levels staying normal in a person whose kidneys have stopped filtering
questions.explanation: A case where water balance holds without kidney function would contradict the claim. The other observations are all consistent with it.

questions.stem: Which plant organ anchors the plant and absorbs water?
questions.explanation: Roots anchor and absorb. Leaves photosynthesise and flowers are for reproduction.

questions.stem: What is the main function of a leaf?
questions.explanation: Leaves are the plant's photosynthetic organ — broad, thin and full of chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Which plant tissue carries water and minerals from the roots upwards?
questions.explanation: Xylem moves water up. Phloem moves dissolved sugars in both directions.

questions.stem: Which plant tissue transports dissolved sugars made in the leaves?
questions.explanation: Phloem carries the products of photosynthesis to wherever they are used or stored.

questions.stem: What are the small pores on the underside of a leaf called?
questions.explanation: Stomata are the pores gases pass through. Villi are in the small intestine, not in plants.
questions.teaching:
A leaf has to solve two problems at once: take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and avoid losing too much water.

Its solution is a set of tiny adjustable pores, mostly on the underside where they are shaded and sheltered. Each is flanked by two guard cells that change shape to open or close it. Open, they let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out; closed, they conserve water. That is why plants wilt in heat — the pores shut to save water, and photosynthesis slows as a result. The waxy cuticle on top reduces loss from the upper surface.

questions.stem: What is the main function of a plant's stem?
options: Supporting the plant and transporting substances between roots and leaves
questions.explanation: The stem holds leaves up to the light and carries the transport tissues between root and leaf.

questions.stem: Which plant organ is responsible for reproduction in flowering plants?
questions.explanation: Flowers house the reproductive structures and attract pollinators.

questions.stem: What is transpiration?
options: The production of glucose in chloroplasts
The loss of water vapour from a plant, mostly through the stomata
The uptake of carbon dioxide by leaves
The movement of sugars in the phloem
questions.explanation: Transpiration is water loss, and the resulting pull is what draws water up the xylem.

questions.stem: Which part of a flower produces pollen?
questions.explanation: Anthers produce pollen; the stigma receives it.
questions.teaching:
Flowers are reproductive structures, and each part has a job in getting pollen from one plant to the ovules of another.

The male parts consist of a stalk topped by a structure where pollen grains are produced and released. The female parts consist of a sticky surface that catches pollen, a tube leading down, and an ovary containing ovules at the base. Petals attract pollinators and sepals protected the bud. Knowing which part produces pollen and which receives it is what makes the whole pollination sequence make sense.

questions.stem: A plant's phloem is damaged but its xylem is intact. What is the most likely effect?
options: The plant loses its ability to take up minerals
Sugars cannot reach the roots, so the roots eventually starve
questions.explanation: Water transport is unaffected, but the roots depend on sugars delivered from the leaves — this is why ring-barking kills a tree.

questions.stem: Which comparison between plant and animal organ systems is correct?
options: Both have transport systems, but a plant's has no pump
Plants have a heart that pumps sap
A plant's xylem carries sugars while its phloem carries water
questions.explanation: Xylem and phloem are genuine transport tissues, but movement comes from transpiration pull and pressure differences, not a pump.

questions.stem: Why does a plant wilt on a hot, windy day even with water in the soil?
options: Transpiration removes water faster than the roots can replace it
The roots stop working above a certain temperature
questions.explanation: Heat and wind both speed evaporation from the leaves. The plant recovers when conditions ease.

questions.stem: How does a root hair cell's structure relate to the root system's function?
options: It anchors the plant in the soil
Its long extension increases surface area for absorbing water and minerals
It stores starch for the whole plant
It photosynthesises to feed the root
questions.explanation: This is the cell-to-organ-to-system link the curriculum asks for: cell shape serves the organ's absorbing role.

questions.stem: Which plant tissue does the same broad job as an animal's circulatory system?
questions.explanation: Both move materials around the organism, though by very different mechanisms.

questions.stem: Guard cells close the stomata during a drought. What is the trade-off?
options: Water is saved, but carbon dioxide cannot enter, so photosynthesis slows
Water is saved with no cost to the plant
Photosynthesis increases while water is saved
questions.explanation: The same pore serves both water loss and gas entry, so closing it is always a compromise.

questions.stem: Why are palisade cells arranged in a tightly packed layer near the top of a leaf?
options: To let gases move through the leaf freely
To transport sugars to the stem
To catch as much light as possible before it passes deeper into the leaf
To reduce water loss from the leaf surface
questions.explanation: Structure follows function: the most photosynthetic cells sit where light is strongest. The loosely packed spongy layer below is what allows gas movement.

questions.stem: A gardener cuts a ring of bark from around a tree trunk. Why does the tree die slowly rather than at once?
options: The tree loses its ability to photosynthesise
Water still rises through the xylem, but sugars can no longer reach the roots
The xylem is destroyed but the phloem keeps working
questions.explanation: Bark removal cuts the phloem, which sits just inside it, while the xylem deeper in the trunk continues to carry water.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best show that water moves up a plant through the xylem?
options: Observing that the leaves are green
Placing a cut stem in dye and finding the dye in the xylem tissue when sectioned
Watching the plant grow taller over a week
Weighing the plant before and after watering
questions.explanation: Tracing a marker to a specific tissue is direct evidence of the pathway. Growth and mass changes do not identify which tissue is involved.

questions.stem: Why is it reasonable to call a leaf an organ?
options: It is the largest part of the plant
It is made of one type of cell
It can survive detached from the plant
It is made of several tissues working together for a shared function
questions.explanation: Epidermis, palisade, spongy mesophyll and vascular tissue combine in one structure — that is exactly what defines an organ.

questions.stem: How does a plant's lack of a pump shape its structure compared with an animal's?
options: It relies on the roots pushing water upward, so the stem needs thick walls to withstand that pressure
It moves water only as fast as the plant grows, so the tissue can be short and is renewed each season
It uses the same vessel for water and sugars, so one wide central tube carries everything the plant needs
It depends on evaporation and a continuous water column, so its transport tissue is a network of narrow tubes
questions.explanation: Narrow xylem vessels keep the water column intact under tension. Break the column and the pull fails — which is why a cut stem must be recut under water.

questions.stem: Which organ produces insulin?
questions.explanation: The pancreas releases insulin into the blood and also supplies digestive enzymes to the small intestine.
questions.teaching:
Some organs have more than one job, and the pancreas is the standard example of an organ that is part of two systems at once.

Its digestive role is to release enzymes into the small intestine. Its other role is hormonal: it monitors blood glucose and releases two hormones that push the level in opposite directions — one lowering it after a meal, one raising it between meals. Type 1 diabetes is a failure of the first of those, which is why it is treated by injecting the hormone. The liver stores glucose but does not produce these hormones.

questions.stem: What is the windpipe properly called?
questions.explanation: The trachea carries air; the oesophagus carries food. They run side by side.

questions.stem: Which blood vessels have the thinnest walls?
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are a single cell thick, which is what makes exchange possible.
questions.teaching:
Three kinds of blood vessel differ in structure because they do different jobs, and the structure follows directly from the job.

Vessels carrying blood away from the heart face high pressure, so they have thick muscular walls. Vessels returning blood at low pressure have thinner walls and valves to stop backflow. And the vessels where exchange actually happens have walls just one cell thick — because oxygen, glucose and waste have to diffuse across them, and any thicker would slow that to a crawl. Their walls are the thinnest in the body for exactly that reason.

questions.stem: What do white blood cells mainly do?
questions.explanation: White cells fight pathogens. Oxygen is carried by red cells and clotting is the platelets' job.

questions.stem: Which system removes urea from the blood?
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter urea out of the blood, forming urine.

questions.stem: What connects muscle to bone?
questions.explanation: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.
questions.teaching:
The words for the body's connective structures sound alike and join different things, so it is worth pinning each one down.

One kind of tough cord attaches a muscle to a bone, so that when the muscle shortens, the bone is pulled. Another kind joins one bone to another across a joint, holding it stable and limiting how far it can move. Cartilage is a third material, smooth and slightly springy, cushioning the ends of bones where they meet. Achilles injuries involve the first kind; a rolled ankle usually damages the second.

questions.stem: Which part of the blood is the liquid that carries cells and dissolved substances?
questions.explanation: Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid. Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying molecule inside red cells.

questions.stem: Which organ stores bile until it is needed?
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile; the gall bladder stores and releases it.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the skeletal system besides support?
options: Protecting organs and allowing movement with muscles
questions.explanation: Bones protect organs, anchor muscles for movement, and also make blood cells in the marrow.

questions.stem: Which structure prevents food entering the trachea when swallowing?
questions.explanation: The epiglottis folds over the airway during a swallow.

questions.stem: Why do capillaries slow blood flow compared with arteries?
options: They are further from the heart
Their combined cross-sectional area is much larger, and slower flow allows more exchange
questions.explanation: The vast branching network spreads the same volume across a much bigger total area. The slowdown is useful — it gives diffusion time.

questions.stem: A person's diaphragm is paralysed. Which system is most immediately affected?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm drives breathing. Without it the chest cavity cannot expand to draw air in.

questions.stem: Which combination shows the nervous and endocrine systems differing?
options: Nerve signals are fast and short-lived; hormones are slower and longer-lasting
Hormones are fast and nerve signals are slow
questions.explanation: Speed and duration are the key contrast. Nerves fire in milliseconds; hormones act over minutes to hours.

questions.stem: Why does the body have both mechanical and chemical digestion?
options: Chemical digestion happens only in the mouth
Breaking food into smaller pieces increases the surface area enzymes can act on
Mechanical digestion alone would be enough
questions.explanation: Chewing and churning multiply the surface available to enzymes, so chemical breakdown proceeds far faster.

questions.stem: Blood entering the kidney differs from blood leaving it. How?
options: Leaving blood carries more glucose than entering blood
Leaving blood has less urea and often less water
questions.explanation: Filtering removes urea and adjusts water. Oxygen is used by the kidney but not removed entirely.

questions.stem: Which observation shows the skeletal and muscular systems working together?
options: Muscles contract and pull on bones across a joint to produce movement
questions.explanation: The pairing is mechanical: muscles supply force, bones supply levers, joints supply pivots.

questions.stem: Why can't a muscle push a bone back to its original position?
options: Bones cannot move in two directions
Muscles are attached at only one end
Muscles only pull, so they work in opposing pairs
questions.explanation: Contraction shortens a muscle, so it can only pull. The biceps and triceps are the standard antagonistic pair.

questions.stem: A student says the lungs 'suck air in'. What is the more accurate description?
options: Air is pumped in by the heart
Chest expansion lowers the pressure inside, so air flows in from outside
The lungs contract to pull air in
The lungs push air out and then refill
questions.explanation: Air moves down a pressure gradient. The lungs are passive — they have no muscle of their own.

questions.stem: Which change would most increase the rate of oxygen delivery to muscles during exercise?
options: An increased heart rate and breathing rate together
questions.explanation: Both systems respond together, which is why they are studied as an interacting pair.

questions.stem: Why is the small intestine long and folded?
options: It produces most of the body's enzymes
It maximises the surface available for absorbing nutrients
It slows food so it can be chewed further
questions.explanation: Length, folds, villi and microvilli all serve the same end — surface area.

questions.stem: A person has damaged villi in their small intestine. What symptom would you predict?
options: Food moves through the gut more slowly than usual
Poor nutrient absorption despite eating normally
Appetite falls because the stomach stays full
questions.explanation: With less absorbing surface, nutrients pass through undigested — which is the mechanism behind coeliac disease.

questions.stem: Why is describing the body as 'a set of independent systems' misleading?
options: The body has only one system
Each system depends on materials, signals or removal services provided by others
questions.explanation: Dividing the body into systems is a teaching convenience. Function is continuous across them: no system works without the others.

questions.stem: Which comparison correctly relates cells, tissues and organs in a plant and an animal?
options: Plant organs are made of a single cell type
Both build organs from tissues, which are built from specialised cells
questions.explanation: The organisational hierarchy is the same in both kingdoms — cells to tissues to organs to systems, plant or animal.

questions.stem: Which organ system carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell?
questions.explanation: Circulation is the delivery network. Respiration collects the oxygen and digestion supplies the nutrients.

questions.stem: Where does the digestion of starch begin?
questions.explanation: Saliva contains an enzyme that starts breaking starch down. Protein digestion begins later, in the stomach.

questions.stem: What is the function of stomach acid?
options: Killing many bacteria and helping enzymes break down protein
questions.explanation: The acid provides the conditions stomach enzymes need and kills much of what arrives with food.

questions.stem: Which structure carries a nerve signal away from the cell body?
questions.explanation: Axons carry signals away; dendrites receive incoming ones.

questions.stem: Which organ system produces sperm and eggs?
questions.explanation: The reproductive system produces gametes, though hormones from the endocrine system control it.

questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs?
questions.explanation: It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, even though that blood is oxygen-poor.

questions.stem: Which system defends the body against disease?
questions.explanation: White blood cells and the lymphatic network do this work.

questions.stem: What are the four chambers of the heart?
questions.explanation: Atria receive blood, ventricles pump it out. Valves separate them but are not chambers.

questions.stem: Where are red blood cells made?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow makes blood cells, which is a second major role for the skeletal system.

questions.stem: Why does the body need a double circulation, through the lungs and then the body?
options: It lets the heart beat more slowly
Blood can be re-pressurised after the lungs, so it reaches the body at full pressure
It allows blood to be filtered twice
It doubles the amount of blood in the body
questions.explanation: Passing through the fine lung capillaries drops the pressure. Returning to the heart restores it for the whole-body circuit.

questions.stem: Which best explains why the heart is described as an organ rather than a tissue?
options: It is built from several tissue types working together for one function
It is larger than a tissue
It is found in the chest
questions.explanation: Muscle, nervous, connective and epithelial tissue combine in the heart — the defining feature of an organ.

questions.stem: Why do nerve signals travel faster than hormone signals?
options: Nerve impulses are electrical along a fixed pathway; hormones travel in the bloodstream
Hormones are larger molecules than nerves
Nerve signals are carried by blood
questions.explanation: A dedicated wired path beats broadcasting through the circulation for speed, though the hormone's effect lasts far longer.

questions.stem: Which observation would show that the digestive and circulatory systems interact?
options: Blood glucose rises after a meal
questions.explanation: A nutrient appearing in the blood after digestion is direct evidence of transfer between the two systems.

questions.stem: A patient cannot produce bile. Which food would be hardest to digest?
questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies fats into small droplets so enzymes can act on them. Without it, fat digestion is slow and incomplete.

questions.stem: Why is the alveoli's surface kept moist?
options: Gases must dissolve before they can diffuse across the membrane
It prevents dust entering the lungs
questions.explanation: Diffusion across the alveolar wall happens in solution, which is why the surface is always moist.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces blood through the heart?
options: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body
Body → left atrium → left ventricle → lungs → right atrium → right ventricle → body
Lungs → right atrium → left ventricle → body
Body → right ventricle → right atrium → lungs → body
questions.explanation: Oxygen-poor blood returns to the right side and goes to the lungs; oxygen-rich blood returns to the left side and goes to the body.

questions.stem: Why does a person breathe deeply for some time after exercise stops?
options: The lungs need to cool down
The heart has stopped beating quickly
The body is still clearing carbon dioxide and restoring oxygen used during exercise
questions.explanation: Recovery breathing continues until the accumulated carbon dioxide is cleared and oxygen stores are replenished.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason a single cell cannot do the job of an organ system?
options: A whole body's demands exceed what one cell's surface and volume can handle
questions.explanation: Scale is the constraint. One cell can serve itself; it cannot supply a body of trillions.

questions.stem: Why does a person at high altitude gradually produce more red blood cells?
options: The heart stops pumping as hard
Lower oxygen availability triggers a response that increases oxygen-carrying capacity
The air is colder at altitude
questions.explanation: The body compensates for thinner air by increasing the carrier, not the pump. It takes weeks, which is why athletes train at altitude in advance.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the enzyme that breaks down protein in the stomach. What reaches the small intestine?
options: Protein already broken down to amino acids, because the stomach has other protein enzymes
Protein in longer chains than usual, leaving more for the pancreatic enzymes to finish
Fat that bile can no longer emulsify, because emulsification happens in the stomach
Carbohydrate that is wholly undigested, because amylase needs stomach acid to work
questions.explanation: Mechanical churning continues and pepsin's chemical step is what fails, so protein arrives in longer chains. The pancreas then does more of the work — which is why blocking this one enzyme does not stop protein being absorbed.

questions.stem: Why is it more accurate to say organ systems 'maintain conditions' than simply 'do jobs'?
options: Much of their activity is continuous regulation — keeping temperature, water and glucose within narrow ranges
Organ systems have no particular jobs
Regulation only happens in the brain
Each system completes its task and then stops until called on again
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the underlying purpose. Breathing, filtering and circulating are all in service of holding internal conditions steady.

questions.stem: Which comparison correctly contrasts a plant's and an animal's response to losing water?
options: A plant wilts as its cells lose turgor; an animal's cells shrink but its body keeps its shape
Neither is affected by water loss
A plant keeps its shape and an animal wilts
Both rely on a skeleton for shape
questions.explanation: The plant's shape depends on water pressure against cell walls; an animal's depends on a skeleton, so dehydration shows up differently.
